newsitem.title: USA: End of Peru crisis damages jailed American's case.
newsitem.headline: End of Peru crisis damages jailed American's case.

text.p: The violent end to the Peruvian hostage crisis did nothing to improve the already slim chances that a U.S. citizen and hundreds of others jailed by anonymous military courts for aiding guerrillas would be retried, U.S. human rights activists said on Thursday.

Lori Berenson of New York was convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment in a military trial by anonymous hooded judges last year for conspiring with the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas to kidnap legislators and trade them for jailed rebels.

MRTA rebels stormed the home of the Japanese ambassador in Lima in December, seizing hundreds of hostages and calling for the release of some 400 jailed comrades and improved prison conditions. The crisis ended after 126 days on Tuesday when commandos raided the residence and freed all but one of the remaining 72 hostages. One died during the rescue operation and all 14 of the mainly teenage rebels were killed.

"I don't think we can expect any miracles," said Roger Rathman, spokesman for the rights group Amnesty International. "Nothing's changed relative to the conditions for political prisoners and the president's position on anti-terrorism and anything seen as opposition to the Peruvian government."

The Clinton administration has repeatedly called for a non-military trial for New York-born Berenson, a 28-year-old with a long history of social activism in Central America before she moved to Peru in the early 1990s.

"The U.S. government should be commended for its efforts to have a re-trial for Lori Berenson but this shouldn't just be about Lori Berenson, the world does not look with glee on trials of thousands of people by hooded judges," Rathman said.
A friend of Berenson's who campaigns on her behalf said the decision by President Alberto Fujimori to end the siege damaged her chances of a retrial or early release.

"The military forces have had their hands strengthened by the violent release of the hostages and the chances for Lori's case receiving serious review from a panel of real judges is less likely than before," said Bill Wedermeyer, a housemate of Berenson's when she was a student at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge, Mass.
